title: Diagnose and correct one loose cabinet handle

sections.title: Understand the distinction
sections.body: A small repair begins with diagnosis and authority, not force. Measurement identifies fit; patching and assembly have their own material and load limits. One tightened handle does not establish competence with structural or electrical work.

sections.title: Complete fictional practice material
sections.body: Complete tabletop paper assembly: base has holes A and B30mm apart center-to-center. Supplied handle H1 has holes 30mm apart; H2 has 40mm. Required screws are the exact two labeled S supplied for H1; no alternative fastener specification is given. Diagram in words: each screw passes from the back of the base through A/B into the corresponding handle hole, with the handle supported. This is a non-load-bearing demonstration, not permission to modify actual cabinetry.

sections.title: Work through the supplied case
sections.body: Select the matching handle and order the assembly steps. Explain why a spinning fastener or absent screw specification stops a live attempt. Keep the existing bounded handle repair as the separate practical route.

sections.title: Try a different case before checking
sections.body: A screw spins without securing the handle. Should a power tool be used to overcome resistance?

checks.title: Compare reasoning and review the supplied result
checks.body: H1 matches 30mm; H2 does not. Align, support and engage only the specified screws gently; do not force mismatch or infer a replacement screw size. Partial: choose H1 without explaining fit. Incorrect: drill new holes to make H2 fit. To progress, measure another low-risk object against its actual assembly instructions; for patching, identify substrate and approved patch method on a scrap sample, inspect adhesion/finish, then obtain suitable guidance before consequential repair.
criteria: Assembly follows supplied parts and authority
A failed check triggers stopping rather than force

checks.title: Check the changed case
checks.body: No. Stop and investigate fit/damage through an appropriate safe route; more force does not establish a sound fastening. Do not use this lesson on safety-critical assemblies.
